subject: DONE s319: open() rejected any mode carrying a PerlIO :layer — `open $fh, '<:encoding(UTF-8)', $file` FAILED
description:
DONE s319.  Found while probing op/print.t t3 — and the probe is the whole
story: the row is described as "print doesn't launder utf8 overlongs", which
sounds like a Unicode-output issue, but PCL was warning
`Unsupported in-memory open mode: <:utf8` and the OPEN was failing.

SCOPE WAS MUCH WIDER THAN THE ROW.  Both open dispatchers — the real-file one
and the in-memory one — compared the WHOLE mode string with `string=`, so ANY
`:layer` suffix matched no arm and open returned false:

    open $fh, '<:utf8',            $file   -> FAILED
    open $fh, '<:raw',             $file   -> FAILED
    open $fh, '<:encoding(UTF-8)', $file   -> FAILED   <-- ubiquitous CPAN code
    open $fh, '<:utf8',            \$s     -> FAILED
    open $fh, '>:utf8',            \$out   -> FAILED

FIX (CLAUDE.md 11 — one place, both callers): `%p-split-open-mode` splits a
mode into base + layers and returns the external format to use.  Both
dispatchers now switch on the BASE mode.  `:raw`/`:bytes` select :latin-1 on
FILE opens — that is the CL spelling of "no translation", one octet per
character; decoding raw bytes as UTF-8 would corrupt or signal, so this is not
cosmetic.  In-memory handles ignore the encoding layer: the scalar already
holds CL characters, so there is nothing to translate.

VERIFIED byte-identical to perl 5.40.3 across <, <:utf8, <:raw,
<:encoding(UTF-8), <:bytes on files; <, <:utf8, <:raw in-memory; and >:utf8
in-memory writes.  Regression test in Pl/t/transpile-test-08.t.

DELIBERATELY NOT DONE — this is layer ACCEPTANCE, not a PerlIO layer MODEL.
Left to task #139, which already says it needs a design call: :crlf, layer
stacking/ordering, binmode() interaction, PerlIO::get_layers introspection, and
byte-exact round-tripping of MALFORMED utf8.

RESIDUE op/print.t t3: now fails for the RIGHT reason and only that reason.
With the open working, PCL emits c3 81 c2 af … where perl emits c1 af … — it
treats the scalar as characters and re-encodes on output, because there is no
per-scalar UTF-8/byte flag.  That is the blessed §Unicode gap, so op/print.t is
registered XDIFF (its only failing row).
